title: Nuclei & Radioactivity
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Nuclear Radius & Constant Density, Mass Defect & Binding Energy Curve, Nuclear Force, Radioactive Decay Law, Half-Life & Mean Life, Parallel Decay, Alpha/Beta/Gamma Decay & Nuclear Fission/Fusion
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: What Holds Protons Together Inside the Nucleus?

Every atomic nucleus ${}_Z^A X$ contains $Z$ positively charged protons and $N = (A - Z)$ neutral neutrons (collectively called $A$ nucleons) packed into a tiny sphere of radius $\sim 10^{-15}\text{ m}$ ($1\text{ femtometre / Fermi}$). Inside this tiny volume, protons repel each other with tremendous Coulomb forces!

What stops the nucleus from exploding instantly? Nature provides the Strong Nuclear Force—the strongest fundamental force in the universe ($\approx 100\times$ stronger than electrostatic repulsion), which acts equally between $p$-$p$, $n$-$n$, and $p$-$n$ at short range ($\sim 1\text{ to } 3\text{ fm}$)!

Atomic Mass Unit ($1\text{ u}$ or $1\text{ amu}$) & Einstein's Energy Equivalence:
  • Definition: $1\text{ u} = \frac{1}{12} \times (\text{Mass of one } {}_6^{12}\text{C atom}) = 1.6605 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$.
  • Einstein Energy Equivalent ($E = \Delta m \cdot c^2$): $$\boxed{1\text{ u}\cdot c^2 = 931.5\text{ MeV}}$$

topics.title: Nuclear Radius ($R = R_0 A^{1/3}$), Constant Nuclear Density, Mass Defect ($\Delta m$), Binding Energy Curve & Nuclear Force
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Nuclear Size ($R$) & Universal Constant Nuclear Density ($\rho_{\text{nuc}}$)

Scattering experiments show that the volume $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3$ of any nucleus is directly proportional to its mass number $A$ (total number of nucleons):

$$\text{Nuclear Radius:} \qquad \boxed{R = R_0 A^{1/3}} \qquad \left(\text{where } R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15}\text{ m} = 1.2\text{ fm}\right)$$
$$\text{Nuclear Matter Density:} \qquad \boxed{\rho_{\text{nuc}} = \frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Volume}} = \frac{A \cdot m_N}{\frac{4}{3}\pi (R_0 A^{1/3})^3} = \frac{3 m_N}{4\pi R_0^3} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}\text{ kg/m}^3}$$

Crucial JEE Fact: Because $A$ cancels out completely in the numerator and denominator, Nuclear Density $\rho_{\text{nuc}}$ is a UNIVERSAL CONSTANT—completely independent of mass number $A$! (A light Helium nucleus and a heavy Uranium-238 nucleus have the exact same nuclear density!).

1.2 Mass Defect ($\Delta m$), Binding Energy ($BE$) & The $BE/A$ Stability Curve
Why Is a Bound Nucleus Always Lighter Than the Sum of Its Constituent Nucleons?
When $Z$ protons and $(A-Z)$ neutrons bind together to form a nucleus ${}_Z^A X$, energy is released as Binding Energy ($BE$), causing the bound nucleus to have less mass than its separate nucleons by the Mass Defect ($\Delta m$):
$$\boxed{\Delta m = \left[Z m_p + (A - Z)m_n\right] - m_{\text{nucleus}}} \qquad \implies \qquad \boxed{BE = \Delta m \cdot c^2 = \Delta m\text{ (in u)} \times 931.5\text{ MeV}}$$
  • Binding Energy per Nucleon ($\frac{BE}{A}$): Measures the stability of a nucleus.
    • For $30 < A < 170$, $BE/A$ is nearly constant at $\approx 8.0\text{ to } 8.8\text{ MeV}$ (proving saturation / short-range nature of nuclear force).
    • Maximum Peak: Occurs for Iron-56 (${}_{26}^{56}\text{Fe}$) and Nickel-62 at $\boxed{\frac{BE}{A} \approx 8.75\text{ MeV}}$ (most stable nuclei in nature!).
    • Why Fission & Fusion Release Energy: Very light nuclei ($A < 20$) undergo Fusion and very heavy nuclei ($A > 200$) undergo Fission so that the daughter products move closer to the middle peak, increasing $BE/A$ and releasing $\boxed{Q = \sum BE_{\text{products}} - \sum BE_{\text{reactants}} > 0}$!
topics.derivationHtml:
How to Calculate Q-Value Using Binding Energies vs. Atomic Masses

1. From Rest Masses (Masses of Reactants Minus Products):

$$\boxed{Q = \left(\sum m_{\text{reactants}} - \sum m_{\text{products}}\right) \times 931.5\text{ MeV}}$$

2. From Binding Energies (BE of Products Minus Reactants — Opposite Order!):
Because $m_{\text{nucleus}} = Z m_p + N m_n - BE/c^2$ (more tightly bound means smaller rest mass!):

$$\boxed{Q = \sum (BE)_{\text{products}} - \sum (BE)_{\text{reactants}}}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap (Sign Reversal Between Mass Formula and Binding Energy Formula for $Q$-Value):
    • When given Rest Masses ($m$): $Q = (m_{\text{initial}} - m_{\text{final}})c^2$ (Initial minus Final).
    • When given Binding Energies ($BE$): $Q = BE_{\text{final}} - BE_{\text{initial}}$ (Final minus Initial)! Never mix up the order!

topics.title: Law of Radioactive Decay, Activity, Half-Life ($T_{1/2}$), Mean Life ($\tau$), Parallel Decay & Simultaneous Production
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Rutherford-Soddy Law of Radioactive Decay
Statistical Law:
Radioactive decay is a spontaneous, random nuclear process (completely unaffected by temperature, pressure, or chemical bonding) in which the rate of disintegration $-\frac{dN}{dt}$ at any instant is directly proportional to the number of undecayed parent nuclei $N(t)$ present at that instant:
$$\boxed{-\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N} \implies \boxed{N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t} = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t / T_{1/2}}}$$
$$\text{Number of Decayed (Daughter) Nuclei at Time } t: \qquad \boxed{N_{\text{decayed}}(t) = N_0 - N(t) = N_0\left(1 - e^{-\lambda t}\right)}$$
$$\text{Activity (Decay Rate):} \qquad \boxed{A(t) = \left|\frac{dN}{dt}\right| = \lambda N(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}} \qquad \left(\text{where } A_0 = \lambda N_0\right)$$

Units of Activity:
• SI Unit: $1\text{ Becquerel (Bq)} = 1\text{ decay/second}$.
• $1\text{ Curie (Ci)} = \mathbf{3.7 \times 10^{10}\text{ Bq}}$; $\quad 1\text{ Rutherford (Rd)} = \mathbf{10^6\text{ Bq}}$.

2.2 Half-Life ($T_{1/2}$), Mean Life ($\tau$), Parallel Decay & Constant Production
$$\text{1. Half-Life:} \quad \boxed{T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \frac{0.693}{\lambda}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{2. Mean (Average) Life:} \quad \boxed{\tau = \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{T_{1/2}}{\ln 2} \approx 1.443\,T_{1/2}}$$

Parallel (Simultaneous) Decay Channels ($\lambda_1, T_1$ and $\lambda_2, T_2$):
If a nucleus can decay simultaneously via two modes (say $\alpha$-decay with constant $\lambda_1$ and $\beta$-decay with constant $\lambda_2$), then $-\frac{dN}{dt} = (\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)N$:

$$\boxed{\lambda_{\text{eff}} = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2} \qquad \implies \qquad \boxed{\frac{1}{T_{\text{eff}}} = \frac{1}{T_1} + \frac{1}{T_2} \iff T_{\text{eff}} = \frac{T_1 T_2}{T_1 + T_2}}$$

Simultaneous Production (at Constant Rate $R_0\text{ nuclei/s}$) and Radioactive Decay ($\lambda$):
Since net rate of change is $\frac{dN}{dt} = R_0 - \lambda N$, starting from $N(0) = 0$:

$$\boxed{N(t) = \frac{R_0}{\lambda}\left(1 - e^{-\lambda t}\right)} \qquad \left(\text{Maximum Secular Equilibrium Number as } t \to \infty: \; \boxed{N_{\max} = \frac{R_0}{\lambda}}\right)$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Probability of Survival vs. Probability of Decay & Small-Time Binomial Approximation (t ≪ T_1/2)

1. Survival & Decay Probabilities in Time $t$:
• Probability that a given nucleus survives for time $t$: $\boxed{P_{\text{survival}} = \frac{N(t)}{N_0} = e^{-\lambda t}}$.
• Probability that a given nucleus decays within time $t$: $\boxed{P_{\text{decay}} = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}}$.

2. Small-Time Approximation ($\lambda t \ll 1$): When $t \ll T_{1/2}$, never waste time computing exponentials! Use $e^{-\lambda t} \approx 1 - \lambda t$, so the fraction decayed in a tiny time $t$ is simply $\boxed{\frac{\Delta N}{N_0} \approx \lambda t}$!

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Rock Dating Ratio $N_{\text{parent}} : N_{\text{daughter}} = 1 : 7$): If the ratio of undecayed parent $A$ to stable daughter $B$ in a rock sample is $1 : 7$, students mistakenly set $N/N_0 = 1/7$! WRONG! Since every daughter nucleus $B$ came from a decayed parent $A$, the original number of parent nuclei was $N_0 = N_A + N_B = 1 + 7 = \mathbf{8}$ parts! Thus $\frac{N}{N_0} = \frac{1}{8} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 \implies \mathbf{t = 3\,T_{1/2}}$!

topics.title: Alpha, Beta ($\beta^-, \beta^+$) & Gamma Decay, Kinetic Energy Sharing in $\alpha$-Decay, Nuclear Fission & Fusion
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Alpha ($\alpha$), Beta ($ eta^-, eta^+$) & Gamma ($\gamma$) Decay Equations
Decay ModeNuclear Transformation EquationKey Energy & Spectrum Features
1. Alpha ($\alpha$) Decay
(Emits ${}_2^4 ext{He}$ nucleus)		$${}_Z^A X \longrightarrow {}_{Z-2}^{A-4} Y + {}_2^4 ext{He} + Q$$Discrete Monoenergetic Spectrum!
By momentum conservation ($p_Y = p_\alpha$):
$$ oxed{K_\alpha = \left( rac{A - 4}{A} ight)Q, \qquad K_Y = \left( rac{4}{A} ight)Q}$$
2. Beta-Minus ($ eta^-$) Decay
(Neutron $ o$ Proton)		$$n o p + e^- + ar{ u}$$
$${}_Z^A X \longrightarrow {}_{Z+1}^A Y + e^- + ar{ u}$$		Continuous Energy Spectrum from $0$ to $Q$ because 3-body decay shares energy with the antineutrino ($ ar{ u}$)!
3. Beta-Plus ($ eta^+$) Decay
(Proton $ o$ Neutron)		$$p o n + e^+ + u$$
$${}_Z^A X \longrightarrow {}_{Z-1}^A Y + e^+ + u$$		Using neutral atomic masses, two electron masses must be subtracted:
$$ oxed{Q_{ eta^+} = \left[M_{ ext{atom}}(X) - M_{ ext{atom}}(Y) - 2m_e ight]c^2}$$
4. Gamma ($\gamma$) Decay
(Excited nucleus de-excites)		$${}_Z^A X^* \longrightarrow {}_Z^A X + \gamma$$No change in $Z$ or $A$! Emits high-energy $\gamma$ photon ($\sim ext{MeV}$).
3.2 Nuclear Fission & Nuclear Fusion
  • 1. Nuclear Fission: Splitting of a heavy nucleus by a slow thermal neutron:
    $$ oxed{{}_{92}^{235} ext{U} + {}_0^1 n \longrightarrow {}_{56}^{141} ext{Ba} + {}_{36}^{92} ext{Kr} + 3\,{}_0^1 n + 200 ext{ MeV}}$$
    ($\approx 0.85 ext{ MeV}$ released per nucleon). Controlled chain reactions in nuclear reactors use Moderators ($ ext{D}_2 ext{O}$ heavy water or graphite to slow down fast neutrons) and Control Rods (Cadmium $ ext{Cd}$ or Boron $ ext{B}$ to absorb excess neutrons).
  • 2. Thermonuclear Fusion (Source of Energy in the Sun & Stars):
    Combining four light protons into a Helium-4 nucleus at ultra-high temperature ($T \sim 10^7 ext{ K}$ to overcome Coulomb barrier): $ oxed{4\,{}_1^1 ext{H} \longrightarrow {}_2^4 ext{He} + 2e^+ + 2 u + 26.7 ext{ MeV}}$ ($\approx 6.7 ext{ MeV}$ per nucleon—$8 imes$ more energy per unit mass than fission!).
topics.derivationHtml:
Proof of Alpha Kinetic Energy Fraction K_α = [(A − 4) / A] Q

When a stationary parent nucleus of mass number $A$ decays into a daughter of mass $m_Y \approx (A-4)u$ and an $\alpha$-particle of mass $m_\alpha \approx 4u$, linear momentum conservation requires $p_\alpha = p_Y$. Since $K = \frac{p^2}{2m} \propto \frac{1}{m}$, kinetic energy divides inversely with mass:

$$\frac{K_\alpha}{K_Y} = \frac{m_Y}{m_\alpha} = \frac{A - 4}{4} \quad \text{and} \quad K_\alpha + K_Y = Q \implies \boxed{K_\alpha = \left(\frac{A - 4}{A}\right)Q, \qquad K_Y = \left(\frac{4}{A}\right)Q}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap (Finding Number of $\alpha$ and $\beta^-$ Particles Emitted in a Decay Chain ${}_{Z_1}^{A_1} X \to {}_{Z_2}^{A_2} Y$):
    1. Always find the number of $\alpha$-particles FIRST from the mass number change (since $\beta$-decay never changes $A$!): $\boxed{n_\alpha = \frac{A_1 - A_2}{4}}$.
    2. Then find the number of $\beta^-$ particles from charge conservation: $Z_1 = Z_2 + 2n_\alpha - n_{\beta^-} \implies \boxed{n_{\beta^-} = 2n_\alpha - (Z_1 - Z_2)}$!

summary:
• Nucleus Size & BE: $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$ ($R_0 = 1.2\text{ fm}$); $\rho_{\text{nuc}} = \text{const}$; $BE = \Delta m(\text{in u}) \times 931.5\text{ MeV}$.
  • Radioactivity: $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t} = N_0(1/2)^{t/T_{1/2}}$; $T_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{\lambda}$; $\tau = \frac{1}{\lambda}$; Parallel $T_{\text{eff}} = \frac{T_1 T_2}{T_1 + T_2}$.
  • Nuclear Decays: $\alpha$-decay $K_\alpha = \frac{A-4}{A}Q$; $n_\alpha = \frac{\Delta A}{4}$ and $n_{\beta^-} = 2n_\alpha - \Delta Z$.
formulaSheetHtml:
ConceptMaster Formula
Nuclear Radius & Density$R = R_0 A^{1/3} \; (R_0 = 1.2\text{ fm}), \qquad \rho_{\text{nuc}} = \text{Constant}$
Binding Energy & $Q$-Value$BE = \Delta m \times 931.5\text{ MeV}, \qquad Q = \sum BE_{\text{prod}} - \sum BE_{\text{react}}$
Decay Law & Half-Life$N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}, \qquad T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = 0.693\,\tau$
Alpha Kinetic Energy$K_\alpha = \left(\dfrac{A - 4}{A}\right)Q, \qquad K_{\text{daughter}} = \left(\dfrac{4}{A}\right)Q$

questions.prompt: If the nuclear radius of ${}_{13}^{27}\text{Al}$ is $3.6\text{ fm}$, what is the nuclear radius of ${}_{52}^{125}\text{Te}$?
questions.explanation: Since $R = R_0 A^{1/3} \propto A^{1/3}$, we have $\frac{R_{\text{Te}}}{R_{\text{Al}}} = \left(\frac{125}{27}\right)^{1/3} = \frac{5}{3} \implies R_{\text{Te}} = \frac{5}{3}(3.6\text{ fm}) = 6.0\text{ fm}$.

questions.prompt: In the radioactive decay chain ${}_{92}^{238}\text{U} \longrightarrow {}_{82}^{206}\text{Pb}$, how many alpha ($\alpha$) particles and beta-minus ($\beta^-$) particles are emitted?

A radioactive sample has a half-life of $T_{1/2} = 20\text{ minutes}$. How much time passes between the instant when $\frac{1}{3}$ of the sample has decayed and the instant when $\frac{2}{3}$ of the sample has decayed?
questions.explanation: Always work with undecayed nuclei! When $\frac{1}{3}$ has decayed, undecayed remaining is $N_1 = \frac{2}{3}N_0$. When $\frac{2}{3}$ has decayed, undecayed remaining is $N_2 = \frac{1}{3}N_0 = \frac{1}{2}N_1$. Since the undecayed amount halved from $\frac{2}{3}N_0$ to $\frac{1}{3}N_0$, the time elapsed is exactly ONE half-life $= 20\text{ minutes}$!

questions.prompt: A radioactive nucleus can decay simultaneously by two different processes which have half-lives $T_1 = 3\text{ hours}$ and $T_2 = 6\text{ hours}$ respectively. What is the effective half-life $T_{\text{eff}}$ of the nucleus?
questions.explanation: For parallel decay modes, $\lambda_{\text{eff}} = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 \implies T_{\text{eff}} = \frac{T_1 T_2}{T_1 + T_2} = \frac{3 \times 6}{3 + 6} = \frac{18}{9} = 2\text{ hours}$.

questions.prompt: A stationary ${}_{88}^{220}\text{Ra}$ nucleus undergoes alpha decay with a total $Q$-value of $5.5\text{ MeV}$. What is the kinetic energy $K_\alpha$ of the emitted alpha particle?
questions.explanation: $K_\alpha = \left(\frac{A - 4}{A}\right)Q = \left(\frac{220 - 4}{220}\right)(5.5\text{ MeV}) = \frac{216}{220} \times 5.5 = \frac{216}{40} = 5.4\text{ MeV}$ (and daughter recoil energy is $0.1\text{ MeV}$).
